topic.title: The price you decide on isn't the price you pay
topic.claim: Food apps show you the dish price to decide and add the fees after you've already decided, because by then you won't back out.
topic.moment: Sunday night, a ₹349 biryani in the cart; at checkout it's ₹462 after delivery, platform, packaging and taxes, and you pay anyway.

turn.believed: The fees are small, honest add-ons; you could always cancel.
turn.actually: They come last on purpose: once you've chosen, waited and imagined eating it, backing out feels like losing the dinner, not saving ₹100.

topic.because: Commitment: the effort already spent choosing makes a late extra cost feel smaller than starting over. Showing fees at the end is called drip pricing, and India's consumer regulator lists it as a dark pattern.
topic.payoff: The menu price is for deciding. The checkout price is for after you've decided.
topic.send_to: the friend who orders in every Sunday
topic.group: anyone who orders food on an app

cover.headline: The low price is to make you [decide]. The fees come after.
cover.sub: Why your food order always jumps at checkout.

paragraphs: The menu price is for deciding. The checkout price is for after you've already decided.
slides.why_swipe: Reader wants to see the trick named.

paragraphs: It's Sunday night. You've scrolled for twenty minutes, closed three places, read other people's reviews.
Finally the biryani goes in the cart. Dinner is settled in your head.
slides.why_swipe: What happens when they tap checkout?

paragraphs: Then you hit checkout. Delivery fee. Platform fee.
A packaging charge. Taxes on top.
The number has climbed. You pause for half a second. Then you tap pay.
slides.why_swipe: Why did you pay instead of backing out?

paragraphs: In your head you were already on the sofa with the box open, the match on, tearing into the first piece.
**By then the extra isn't a cost. It's the price of not starting the hunt over.**
slides.why_swipe: Is this an accident or built on purpose?

paragraphs: It has a name: drip pricing. India's consumer regulator lists it as a dark pattern.
The cheap menu number had one job, and it did it. It got you to commit.
slides.why_swipe: So what's the one line to remember?

paragraphs: Count how many times the fees made you close the app and cook instead. For most people it's zero.
Next Sunday you'll still order. **You'll just stop believing the menu.**

end.save: Open it the next time your cart grows between the menu and the pay button.
end.send: Send to the friend who orders in every single Sunday.
end.promise: How things really get sold to us.

claims.text: India's consumer regulator (the CCPA) has officially classified drip pricing as a dark pattern.
claims.sentence: India's consumer regulator lists it as a dark pattern.

claims.text: Drip pricing is a defined pricing practice: a low headline price is shown upfront to secure commitment, while mandatory extra charges are disclosed only later, at checkout.
claims.sentence: It has a name: drip pricing.

claims.text: Mechanism: (1) the menu price's function is to get the customer to decide/commit; (2) delivery, platform, packaging fees and taxes are revealed only after that decision, at checkout; (3) this sequencing is the recognized practice of drip pricing, which regulators classify as a dark pattern; therefore (4) the low menu price is not the real price but a device to lock in commitment before the true cost is shown, exploiting the fact that by checkout, abandoning the order feels costlier than paying the extra fees.
claims.sentence: The menu price is for deciding. The checkout price is for after you've already decided. ... It has a name: drip pricing. India's consumer regulator lists it as a dark pattern. The cheap menu number had one job, and it did it. It got you to commit.

India's consumer regulator (the CCPA) ha.correct: India's CCPA notified the Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023 on 30 November 2023 under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, listing 13 specified dark patterns, one of which is 'Drip Pricing.' This remains in force as of the Oct 25, 2026 go-live date, so the claim is timelessly true, not merely current.

sources.quote: elements of prices not revealed upfront or revealed surreptitiously within the user experience

drip pricing is defined as "a practice whereby- elements of prices are not revealed upfront or are revealed surreptitiously within the user experience; or revealing the price post-confirmation of purchase, i.e., charging an amount higher than the amount disclosed at the time of checkout..."

mechanism.broken_premise: None fails. Minor nuance: fees are disclosed at the checkout/cart screen before payment is confirmed, so the lock-in is psychological (completion/sunk-cost bias), not financial or contractual concealment after purchase. Also, GST (5% on restaurant food) is statutory and must be itemized, so 'taxes on top' is lawful disclosure, not part of the manipulation. Neither undercuts the take, which the post itself frames behaviorally.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: The menu price excludes delivery, platform and packaging fees plus GST; these appear itemized at the cart/checkout before you tap pay, so you can still abandon for free at that point. India's CCPA Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023 define drip pricing to include prices 'not revealed upfront,' which captures this exact pattern, and classify it as an unfair trade practice. The real trap is the completion/sunk-cost bias the post describes: by checkout you've mentally committed, so the fee feels cheaper than restarting the search.

sources.quote: Drip pricing: a practice whereby elements of prices are not revealed upfront or are revealed surreptitiously within the user experience; or revealing the price post-confirmation of purchase.
The Guidelines identify thirteen dark patterns, including drip pricing, and classify them as unfair trade practices subject to action under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
Food delivery services frequently engage in drip pricing, with fees presented at various times in the shopping process and often revealed only right before checkout.
